reason: The subprocess seam is kept as a Go contract package: lookup, Start and StartTerminal from a fully explicit spec, never a shell string. It changes in three ways: a required launch plan, a stop ladder inside the seam, and an outcome that records why a run was stopped.

The local provider is kept as the component that wraps the single process package. Tree owners are held by the host itself (job object, control group, process group) instead of a helper Node process and a systemd-run scope per command; collectors spill to the storage area; terminals are allocated by own code instead of node-pty.

The package exists to bind Win32 process, stdio and job-object calls through the koffi foreign-function library. Go calls the same functions through golang.org/x/sys/windows inside the process package, with no binding table, layout probe or separate library package.

The owner-scoped session service is kept: ids minted by the service, publication only after backend setup, one send at a time, every operation fenced to the owner, awaited cleanup. It gains Resize and Attach so a browser can view a session.

The persistent shell backend for bash and pwsh is kept, with two changes: the model reads the emulated screen instead of a hand-written byte filter, and readiness compares screen text and command brackets instead of raw bytes after a marker.

The shell executor contract is kept (request resolved to an explicit spec, one execution with foreground and background views) and becomes a registry by dialect so bash and pwsh can both be mounted. The text exit-marker parser is replaced by structured result fields.

The managed DSH_ environment registry is kept with declared keys, conflict detection and refusal of undeclared output. Built-in variables become the first contributor so the list is complete, and DSH_NODE_EXECUTABLE becomes DSH_EXECUTABLE because there is no Node runtime.

The fresh bash -c executor is kept with its budgets and first-cause classification. It is no longer an unconfined variant: the one bash provider asks the sandbox seam for a launch plan on every call, and it resolves bash on Windows as well.

A separate sandboxing executor exists upstream because confinement is chosen by which package is mounted. In Go confinement is a required field of every spawn for an agent, so this package folds into the one bash provider and the confined-launch path of the process package.

The fresh pwsh -Command executor is kept with its resolution order, UTF-8 preamble and budgets. Commands that must begin with param, using or #requires are run from a private script file, and the provider always requests a launch plan.
As with the bash twin, the sandboxing PowerShell executor exists only because confinement was a choice of provider. It folds into the one pwsh provider, which obtains a launch plan for every call.

The one-shot bash tool is kept with the same arguments, job registration and promotion on timeout. Its result gains structured fields for exit code, stop cause, working directory, truncation and sandbox facts, from which the text markers are rendered.

The one-shot pwsh tool is kept as the PowerShell twin of the bash tool, sharing one tool package and the structured result. The Windows sandbox facts in its description come from what the backend reports instead of a hard-coded gate.

The per-agent persistent bash tool is kept. Commands are delivered by file and bracketed by a nonce instead of being typed into the line editor, the result is read from the emulated screen, and a timed-out shell is interrupted and verified before it is reset.

The per-agent persistent PowerShell tool is kept as the twin of the persistent bash tool and uses the same file delivery, nonce brackets and interrupt-then-verify rule, which removes its echo, ESC and prompt-redefinition limits.

Upstream transports that own their spawn cannot use the service. In Go no package except the process package may import os/exec or call a process-creation function, and the MCP, SDK and plugin transports are harness code that calls it; a source check enforces this.

Each upstream consumer rebuilds its own teardown ladder. The Go seam ships one stop ladder (revoke authority, ask, close input, terminate, kill, then a bounded wait) with a hook for the consumer's protocol-level request.

Consumers no longer need to know the provider to learn how strongly a tree is owned: every handle and result reports its owner kind. The weaker rungs that remain on macOS and on Linux without a control group are carried under the subprocess-local limits.

Disposal can wait for ever upstream after SIGKILL. The Go stop ladder ends with a settle deadline: past it, Stop returns an error naming the survivors, the handle stays registered and the fiber unload completes with the leak reported.

An owner kept by the operating system still needs a host facility. The requirement is narrower than upstream: no systemd-run version rules, only cgroup v2 with a writable own subtree on Linux; macOS still has no persistent owner.
justification: No design choice can give macOS a persistent process-range owner, and a Linux control group needs a writable cgroup v2 subtree. The weaker rung is selected once, announced once and reported on every handle, and its survivors are documented.

reason: Upstream probes with child processes on every eligible spawn and keeps a runner per command. The Go provider decides its owner rung once when it starts, by checking that it can create a control group or job object, and uses no child process to probe or to hold an owner.

The process is created inside its job in the same CreateProcess call through the job-list attribute, the host holds the only job handle, and the job grants no breakaway, so the create-to-assign window and the breakaway exclusion are removed. This is an inference to be confirmed by the Windows tree scenario.

On Windows an interrupt is still the Ctrl-C input byte, which the console delivers to every attached process, and stop and hang-up do not exist. The Go design refuses the unsupported signals instead of ignoring them.
justification: Windows consoles have no per-process-group job-control signals, so no terminal library can deliver them. The limit is an operating-system fact and is stated in the tool results and the specification.

reason: Go terminals use the operating system's ConPTY by default and need no file beside the binary; an operator may configure a console host directory. The reason for bundling, a byte comparison of the prompt, is removed by comparing the emulated screen.

On macOS, and on Linux without a control group, a child that leaves the terminal session before it is observed can still escape cleanup. Where a control group or job object is available the terminal is inside it and the gap is closed.
justification: Process groups and sessions are the strongest owners macOS offers, and scanning the process table only sees a moment. Owning the master descriptor improves what is observed, not what can be guaranteed.

reason: Go runs no code at exit, so cleanup does not depend on an observable exit: a Windows job handle closes with the host, Linux direct children get a parent-death signal, and the host handles SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP by unloading its tree. What survives a killed host on Linux and macOS is stated per system.

The scrub is still based on names. It is reduced: deny and allow patterns are configuration, PASSPHRASE and CREDENTIAL join the defaults, and every name the configuration uses as a credential reference is removed exactly.
justification: The harness cannot know which ambient variables hold secrets it never read, so a secret with an unusual name in the operator's environment still reaches a child. The security foundation accepts this residual explicitly.

reason: Spill output is written through the storage area's spill store, which owns retention, instead of into an unowned directory under the operating-system temp folder, so completed spill files are collected.
The process package no longer creates a per-process spill directory once; each spill asks the storage area's store for a writer, and that store owns and recreates its directory.

The limit is about resolving a koffi binding table that loads Windows DLLs at import time. Go selects Windows code with build constraints at compile time and has no foreign-function loader, so it exists only because of the Node binding.
The Win32 primitives become private functions of the process package, and the subprocess service around them is the only API, so no consumer has to assemble policy, limits and handle closure itself.

The null environment block is a workaround for koffi failing to marshal an explicit block. Go passes an explicit sorted UTF-16 block with CREATE_UNICODE_ENVIRONMENT, so the limit exists only because of the JavaScript binding.
There is no standalone primitive package any more: streams, handles, output policy and cancellation are owned by the one process package that contains the primitives.

Creating the process inside its job in one call removes the interval between creation and assignment in which a suspended target could be left behind. The suspended-create fallback keeps the old window and is reported when used.

The architecture-specific header probe guards hand-written structure layouts for koffi. golang.org/x/sys/windows supplies typed structures per architecture, so there is no layout to probe; it exists only because of the JavaScript binding.
Terminal sessions and their screen state still live only in the host process and end with it; the model's input and returned output stay durable through the tool events.
justification: Surviving a host restart needs an owner outside the host process with its own protocol, and the tree owners deliberately end children with the host. Durable work belongs in files.

reason: A session still has exactly one owner and no other agent can use it. A person may attach a browser to it, which is access decided by the host route, not a transfer of ownership.
justification: Owner scoping is the access rule that keeps one agent out of another agent's terminal; sharing between agents would need a separate authority contract that nothing asks for.

reason: Sessions are still created only on request, by an agent tool call or by a user through the web terminal; configuration cannot start one.
justification: A session needs an owner whose end closes it, and an owner exists only once an agent or user asks. A terminal started from configuration would be a shared global resource with no owner.

reason: The model reads lines from the host-side emulated screen, which follows the alternate screen, so a full-screen program's current page is readable. This holds once the emulator gate passes; if the gate ends on the line-screen fallback the limit returns and is recorded.

Readiness is narrower but not exact everywhere: a bracketed command completes exactly on every system and shell-at-prompt is exact on Linux and macOS, while proving that a foreign child waits for input stays possible on Linux only.
justification: No portable kernel facility proves that another process is blocked reading the terminal; macOS and Windows offer none. The wait reason keeps the uncertainty visible as inferred_idle.

reason: The PowerShell bootstrap writes its prompt marker with core types only and pins the code page with chcp, both allowed in ConstrainedLanguage, so it no longer depends on Console static calls. This is an inference proven by the Windows terminal scenario under read-only mode.
The split is kept as the design and made explicit: tree teardown is one Close operation owned by the process package, and the backend only calls it and awaits it.
A host restart still destroys every terminal session, for the same reason as the service-level limit.
justification: Restoration needs an out-of-process owner and a versioned protocol; the tree owners end children with the host on purpose so nothing runs unowned.

reason: There is no unconfined executor in Go. The one bash provider must put a launch plan from the sandbox seam on every spawn made for an agent, and the process package refuses such a spawn without one.
A persistent shell exists as its own tool on the terminal seam; the one-shot executor stays stateless on purpose.

The bash provider resolves its program by stated rules on every system, including Git for Windows on Windows while skipping the WSL launchers, and tree semantics come from the job object, so bash is no longer POSIX-only.
A start failure is an explicit Failed outcome carrying the error, separate from the output streams, so it is not served as a synthetic stderr stream that a consuming reader can lose.
Confinement still governs file effects first; the network is restricted only where a backend can enforce the resolved network policy, and process visibility is not uniform.
justification: The security model states this narrow guarantee on purpose and the sandbox area owns it; a shell executor cannot widen what the operating-system backends enforce.

reason: Whether the launcher failed is now a fact read from its status record, but a denied file operation is still inferred from the failed command's stderr and is reported only as a hint.
justification: No sandbox backend reports an individual denied file operation out of band, so the classification can still be wrong in both directions; the result field is named a hint for that reason.

reason: Start returns only after the launcher status record, so a launcher that fails is a start error for a background run as well, not a fact discovered on a later read of the job.

The executor never bypasses the sandbox seam: the seam is asked for every call and itself returns the unconfined plan for danger-full-access, so one place decides and the fact is recorded on the outcome.
As for bash, there is no unconfined PowerShell executor: the one pwsh provider must carry a launch plan on every spawn made for an agent.
A persistent PowerShell exists as its own tool on the terminal seam; the one-shot executor stays stateless on purpose.
The command is still PowerShell text passed as one argument and parsed by PowerShell, so a syntax error is a command failure and not a launch failure.
justification: This is what a shell tool is: it hands text to that shell. Parsing the command in the harness would duplicate the shell and could disagree with it.

reason: A start failure is an explicit Failed outcome carrying the error, separate from the output streams, as for the bash provider.

The outcome records the stop cause the harness itself applied (timeout, cancelled, user, owner gone), so a stopped Windows process is classified without a signal. A kill from outside the harness still looks like an ordinary exit, which is stated as a residual.
A command whose first statement is param, using or #requires is written to a private script file and invoked after the encoding preamble, so the preamble no longer breaks it.
Non-ASCII standard input can still be mis-decoded when the resolved shell is Windows PowerShell 5.1, because its input encoding cannot be set under redirected input.
justification: It affects only the 5.1 fallback and only trusted in-process callers that pass stdin, which the model-facing tool does not expose. The executor reports the edition so such a caller can refuse, and the fallback can be disabled by configuration.

reason: Reads remain unconfined on Windows under the restricted-token backend the Go design keeps.
justification: The security model lists unconfined reads as a residual gap of every platform and of the Windows backend in particular; the sandbox area owns the backend and reports enforcement as partial.

reason: The private temp directory for workspace-write is kept as behaviour and has a defined carrier: the launch plan from the sandbox area holds the TMP and TEMP edits and the process package applies them.
Windows read-only mode remains a partial boundary (hard links, unconfined reads, trees with package-specific access entries) under the backend the Go design keeps.
justification: The design states that Windows enforcement is always partial and reports it on every result; removing the gap needs a different Windows mechanism, which is the sandbox area's decision.

reason: Built-in variables are registered as the first contributor with their descriptions, so List returns every managed variable and can feed the generated catalog.
Feeding a running program is the terminal seam's contract (Send on an owned session); the one-shot shell seam stays without it on purpose, so the vocabulary exists where the state lives.
The executor owns no timer. The caller's context carries the only deadline with a typed cause, so a caller-owned deadline is the normal mode and not a deferred one.
The persistent tool still needs an owning agent and a real pseudo-terminal; where none can be allocated it reports unavailable.
justification: The owner is what gives the shell a lifetime and an access rule, and persistent shell state needs a terminal; a call with no agent has nothing to scope the shell to.

reason: A foreground child that waits for input is still recognised exactly only on Linux; elsewhere the call runs to its timeout, after which the shell is interrupted and usually kept.
justification: Proving that a foreign process is blocked reading the terminal needs a kernel facility that macOS and Windows do not offer. A following command is refused while the previous one has not finished, so nothing is typed into the child.

reason: A timeout or cancellation first interrupts the foreground group and keeps the shell when the end line and prompt then appear; only a shell that cannot be verified is reset. An explicit exit still ends the shell, as asked.
The description stays a config field for deployment facts, and the tool adds the facts it resolved itself (shell path and edition) so they do not have to be written by hand.
The command text is written to a file and evaluated by a bootstrap function; only a fixed short line is typed, so TAB, ESC and DEL in a command never reach the line editor.

Exit code, signal and stop cause are structured fields of the logged result, and the text marker is rendered from them, so output that happens to end with a marker-shaped line cannot change the status shown.
The tool has no executor timer to opt out with: its timeout is a deadline on the call's context, the same mechanism every tool uses.

A timeout given for a background run applies to it, a deployment cap on background runtime exists, and the owner's end always stops the job, so a background command is no longer unbounded by construction.
The job registration carries the id of the tool call that is waiting on it, so a task list can mark those rows; the field is requested from the jobs area.
The persistent PowerShell tool still needs an owning agent and a pseudo-terminal backend with the pwsh dialect; where none exists it reports unavailable.
justification: As for the bash twin, the owner gives the shell its lifetime and access rule, and persistent shell state needs a terminal.

reason: Only a short fixed line is typed, printed before the start line of the command bracket, and the result is the screen text between the bracket lines, so echoed input cannot leak into a result.
The command is read from a file by the bootstrap function and never passes through PSReadLine, so a raw ESC in a command is supported.
A command completes on the end line that carries its own nonce, printed by the bootstrap function, so redefining the prompt function does not remove the completion signal.
A new command is refused while the previous one has not printed its end line, so a child that reads input cannot consume the next call's command; the model interrupts or restarts instead.
Stop and hang-up are still unavailable on Windows and an interrupt is a console-wide Ctrl-C, which at a prompt cancels the pending line.
justification: Windows consoles have no per-process-group signals; the backend refuses the unsupported signals and the result says so.

reason: The bootstrap uses core types and chcp only, so it succeeds when the read-only Windows sandbox starts PowerShell in ConstrainedLanguage. This is an inference proven by the Windows terminal scenario.
A terminal bell is still not reported to the model; the prompt marker stays a readiness signal consumed by the host.
justification: Nothing consumes a bell event, and adding a model-facing channel for terminal decoration would spend tokens without a use.

reason: Under the Windows sandbox read-only PowerShell still starts in ConstrainedLanguage and confined commands still cannot open named pipes.
justification: Both are properties of the Windows restricted-token backend, owned by the sandbox area. The tool keeps teaching them, now from the facts the backend reports for the call.

reason: The persistent PowerShell tool is part of the design and keeps one owner-scoped shell alive across calls.
The model must still write PowerShell for the pwsh tool and bash for the bash tool; nothing translates between dialects.
justification: Translation between shell languages cannot be made correct in general. Both tools may be mounted on one system, so the model can choose the dialect it needs.

reason: The marker asks to evaluate persistent shell state. The Go design has persistent bash and pwsh tools on the terminal seam, and the one-shot executor stays stateless by decision.
The marker asks for built-ins in list(). In Go the built-in variables are the first contributor, so the list is complete before any consumer treats it as a catalog.
The clipping notice no longer advises a file search; it says how much was cut and how to read the rest, because command output is not a file.
The result reports the recorded stop cause, a timeout, and no longer guesses at an out-of-memory condition the signal does not establish.
The marker asks for an explicit infrastructure-failure outcome on the process handle. The Go execution has a Failed outcome distinct from a kill and from a non-zero exit, and it maps to a failed job.

The marker says deployment policy belongs in the tool pipeline and in confinement. In Go policy listeners sit in the guarded pipeline and every spawn for an agent carries a launch plan, so the tool holds no policy.
The clipping notice of the persistent pwsh tool is the same shared notice as the bash twin and no longer advises a file search.
The persistent pwsh tool reports the recorded stop cause, a timeout, without the unsupported out-of-memory guess.
As for the bash tool, the explicit Failed outcome of an execution replaces the signal-less kill that hid a start failure.
The outer abort race around session start-up does not exist in Go: start-up runs inside the session under one context, and cancelling it rolls the session back.
The per-send fields the marker wants consolidated become one send-state value owned by the session's pump goroutine, so there is no shared mutable send state to coordinate.
The marker asks for a generation boundary so a delayed prompt cannot settle a later send. Each bracketed command carries its own nonce and completes only on the end line with that nonce.

The Go harness exposes a one-shot bash tool with the same arguments (description, command, timeoutMs, workdir, and run_in_background and the escalation pair when available). The result adds structured fields beside the text markers.
The Go harness exposes a one-shot pwsh tool as the PowerShell twin of bash, with the same arguments and structured result; its description states the resolved shell edition.
The Go harness exposes a persistent bash tool under the same name, mounted instead of the one-shot component. It keeps the command argument and adds optional timeoutMs and restart.
The Go harness exposes a persistent pwsh tool under the same name, mounted instead of the one-shot component, with the command argument and optional timeoutMs and restart.

Replaced by the Go struct shell/bash.Config: Path, Timeout, MaxTimeout, TailBytes, SpillBytes and Grace with upstream's defaults. The default directory is the session's current directory, not a config field.
The sandboxing executor's config is the local executor's fields verbatim; with one bash provider there is one struct, shell/bash.Config.
Replaced by the Go struct shell/pwsh.Config: the bash fields plus Path for the PowerShell program and AllowWindowsPowerShell for the 5.1 fallback.
The sandboxing PowerShell executor's config is the local one verbatim; with one pwsh provider there is one struct, shell/pwsh.Config.
The only field, dshHome, selects the harness home. In Go the home is a boot fact that the registry reads from the boot area, so the registry component has no config struct of its own.

Replaced by the Go struct terminal/shellpty.Config: dialect, program and arguments, grid size, scrollback rows, read size, send timeout, silence and grace periods including PromptTailGrace, and an optional console host directory. Poll intervals are not settings.
Replaced by the Go struct shell/tools.OneShotConfig: EnableBackground, PromoteOnTimeout and a new MaxBackgroundRuntime cap.
The pwsh tool uses the same Go struct as the bash tool, shell/tools.OneShotConfig, since the two tools mirror each other.
Replaced by the Go struct shell/tools.PersistentConfig: Backend, Timeout, MaxTimeout, OutputBytes and Description.
The persistent pwsh tool uses the same Go struct as the persistent bash tool, shell/tools.PersistentConfig.

ctx.shell becomes the service key shellexec.Key (shell.Key is the page shell's key in the UI area), a registry of Executor values by dialect (Dialect, Resolve, Start), so bash and pwsh providers can be mounted together.
ctx.shellEnv becomes the service key shellenv.Key with Register, Collect and a complete List; a contributor's entries leave with its fiber.

ctx.subprocess becomes the interface subprocess.Service (World, Lookup, Start, StartTerminal) under the key subprocess.Key for the execution world and subprocess.HostKey for children that must run on the host machine.
ctx.terminals becomes the interface terminal.Service under terminal.Key: Open, Send, Read, Signal, Resize, Attach, Close and List, each taking the owner.

Final verdict after reading the note: keep. The filesystem and subprocess services define one execution world, the terminal primitive belongs to the subprocess provider and readiness to the consumer; this is what lets an SSH provider replace the world without second shell or terminal packages.

Final verdict: change. The fixed descriptor 7 and the C-runtime descriptor table exist for a Node child, and the consumer of the channel, the program guest, is not built. The remaining need, a private inherited byte channel such as the launcher status pipe, is met by generic extra channels in the spawn spec.

Final verdict: keep, narrowed. The two-chunk prompt delivery comes from the Windows console layer, so the setting is kept with default zero. It now matters only for raw sends, because a bracketed command completes on its end line without waiting for the prompt.

Final verdict: change. The note bundles a console host because older system hosts repaint the prompt in another byte form and readiness compared bytes. The Go design compares the emulated screen, where both forms are equal, and uses the system ConPTY; a different host is operator configuration.

Final verdict: keep and extend. Owner-scoped persistent terminal sessions are kept with the same ownership and send rules; reading goes through the emulated screen, which lifts the line-only limit, and the six terminal tools are specified by the experimental area that owns their package.

Final verdict: keep. The Go design ships no E2B backend, and its subprocess and terminal contracts take a context on every call and promise nothing a remote provider cannot give, so a remote world can be added without changing tools.

Final verdict: not adopted. The proposal removes descriptions and list() because nothing reads them. The Go design generates catalogs from running registries, which gives the list a reader, so it keeps the descriptions and completes the list instead.
